name: Structured Logging
intent: Write logs as machine-readable events with named fields and a correlation id, so that you can search, count and follow a request across services instead of reading text.
scenario: A customer reports that their payment failed at 14:03. The system has six services and millions of log lines. Finding the lines about that one customer's request is the whole job.
problem: Free-text logs are written for a person reading one file. At scale they are searched with pattern matching, which finds unrelated lines, misses lines worded differently, and cannot follow one request through many services. Logs that leak passwords or personal data create a second problem.

howItWorks.title: Log events with fields, not sentences
howItWorks.text: Instead of 'Payment failed for user 42 on order 7', write a record such as { level: error, event: payment_failed, user_id: 42, order_id: 7, reason: card_declined }. Each field can be filtered, counted and grouped exactly, and the message stays the same wording so it is easy to find.

howItWorks.title: Use a correlation (trace) id on every line
howItWorks.text: Generate an id when a request enters the system and pass it on every call (in a header). Every log line from every service includes it. Searching that one id returns the whole story of the request in order, across all services.

howItWorks.title: Choose levels deliberately
howItWorks.text: ERROR means something failed and needs attention, WARN means something unexpected that was handled, INFO records normal business events, and DEBUG is detail you turn on when investigating. If everything is ERROR or everything is INFO, the levels carry no information, and the volume (and cost) explodes.

howItWorks.title: Ship logs to a central place
howItWorks.text: Services write to standard output and an agent forwards logs to a central store with search (Elasticsearch, Loki, a cloud logging service). Local files on servers that are replaced every day are no use to an investigator. Set retention, because storage and indexing are expensive.

howItWorks.title: Never log secrets, and be careful with personal data
howItWorks.text: Passwords, tokens, card numbers and health data must not appear in logs, since logs are copied widely and kept for months. Redact or omit sensitive fields at the logger, and log ids instead of personal details.

pros: Exact searches and counts instead of fragile text matching
One id follows a request across every service
Easy to turn into metrics and dashboards (count events by field)
Consistent fields make tooling and alerting possible
cons: Logs are large and costly to store and index at scale
Needs discipline: names and fields drift between teams without conventions
Less readable by eye than a plain sentence, so tools are needed
Easy to leak sensitive data into a widely copied store
whenToUse: Any service that runs in production, especially with several services or instances
Events you will want to count or filter later: errors, payments, logins
When you need to answer 'what happened to this one request?'
whenNotToUse: As a replacement for metrics: counting millions of events in logs is expensive, use a metric
Logging every detail at INFO 'just in case' with no retention plan
pitfalls: Log lines with no request or correlation id
Putting variable data inside the message text, so every line is unique and cannot be grouped
Logging secrets, tokens or full request bodies
Different services using different names for the same field (userId, user, uid)
